notes.meaning: All the military leaders and the surviving people came together to see Jeremiah. After the governor Gedaliah was murdered, they were terrified of what the Babylonians might do to them. Even though they had largely ignored Jeremiah for years, they now turned to him for help.

The leaders begged Jeremiah to pray to God for the tiny group that was left. They pointed out how few people had survived the fall of Jerusalem, hoping to move Jeremiah to pity. They asked him to plead with God as an accepted prophet whose prayers carried great weight.

The people asked Jeremiah to find out which direction they should travel and what they should do next. In reality, they were already leaning heavily toward fleeing to Egypt to escape danger. They hoped God would simply approve the plan they had already made.

Jeremiah agreed to take their request to the Lord in prayer. He reminded them that the Lord was their God too, so they owed Him total obedience. He promised to deliver God's answer honestly without hiding or changing a single word.

The people made a solemn promise before God that they would carry out everything the Lord said through Jeremiah. They called on God Himself to act as their witness and judge if they broke their word. Taking such an oath bound them completely to accept whatever answer came.

The crowd insisted they would obey God's voice whether His command seemed pleasant or hard. They acknowledged that doing what God said was the only way things would go well for them. True obedience means following God even when His instructions go against our personal wishes.

God did not give Jeremiah an answer right away, but waited ten full days before speaking to him. This showed that Jeremiah could not invent prophecies whenever he wanted, but had to wait on God. The delay also gave the people time to calm their panic and test their willingness to obey.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some nineteenth-century critical scholars suggested Jeremiah spent ten days thinking things through and gathering news before offering his own seasoned judgment.

notes.meaning: Once the Lord spoke, Jeremiah gathered the commanders and the entire remnant together so everyone would hear. He began by reminding them that they were the ones who had sent him to present their plea before the God of Israel. Because they asked for God's guidance, they had a sacred duty to listen.

God promised that if the people stayed in Judah, He would establish them safely like a sturdy building or a well-rooted plant. When the Lord said He relented, it meant He was ready to stop bringing disaster and begin showing them mercy instead. His justice had punished their past sins, and now He wanted to heal the land.

The Lord told the people not to be terrified of the king of Babylon, even though they dreaded his revenge. God assured them of His personal presence to protect them and rescue them from Babylonian power. When God is on our side, no human ruler can destroy us.

God promised to show compassion to the people by softening the heart of the Babylonian king toward them. Because the hearts of all rulers are in God's hands, the king would treat them kindly and allow them to settle peaceably in their own homes. Staying in the land would bring the very peace they longed for.

The Lord uncovered the rebellion brewing in their hearts before they even spoke it aloud. They were dreaming of Egypt as a place of rich food and quiet safety where they would never see war or hear trumpet blasts. By believing Egypt could keep them safer than God could, they treated the Lord's promise as untrustworthy.

Jeremiah called directly on the remnant of Judah to hear the stern warning of the Almighty. Setting their faces toward Egypt meant they had formed a stubborn, settled plan to leave. God warned them that refusing to stay in the Promised Land would bring catastrophic consequences.

God warned that the very war and starvation they feared in Judah would chase them down in Egypt. Running away from duty to escape suffering never works, because God's judgment easily reaches into any hiding place. Disobedience would lead to the exact deaths they were trying to avoid.

Every person who stubbornly chose to settle in Egypt was marked for death by warfare, hunger, or disease. Not a single person who made that willful choice would escape the coming ruin. When people run from God's protection, they walk straight into disaster.

Just as the people had seen Jerusalem destroyed by God's anger, the same wrath would pour out on them in Egypt. They would become a horrifying spectacle and a shameful curse-word among the nations, never to see their homeland again. God's past judgments should have warned them that His threats always come true.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators suggest verses 15 through 18 were added later by an editor rather than spoken in Jeremiah's original message.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah gave them a clear, final command from the Lord telling them not to step foot in Egypt. He made it plain that he had solemnly testified to them before God so they could never claim they did not know. When truth is clearly told, those who disobey are left without any excuse.

Jeremiah exposed their deep hypocrisy in asking for prayer when they had already made up their minds. They had promised with fine words to do whatever God commanded, but it was only a show to get God's stamp on their plans. In trying to deceive the prophet and God, they had only succeeded in cheating themselves to their own ruin.

Jeremiah told them that although he had faithfully shared God's complete message that very day, they had already refused to obey it. The prophet could see their stubborn resistance even before they set out on the road. God knows our hearts and sees our rebellion long before we act on it.

The chapter closes with a final, certain sentence of death against the rebellious remnant. War, starvation, and plague would wipe them out in Egypt, the very sanctuary they had chosen for themselves. Seeking safety outside of God's will always ends in tragic loss.
